distinguishing_feature: Both can present with fever and rash; recent drug exposure plus eosinophilia/systemic organ involvement favors DRESS.
Viral exanthem can mimic drug eruption; medication timeline and systemic features help distinguish.
The distinction is mainly whether the viral cause/clinical syndrome is specified.
Both are nonscarring hair-loss categories; the specified category should be used when the cause/pattern is documented.
Unspecified nonscarring hair loss remains a fallback when the documented cause/pattern cannot be specified.
[LLM DRAFT] Well-demarcated plaques with silvery-white scales typically affecting extensor surfaces
[LLM DRAFT] Intense nocturnal pruritus with burrows in web spaces and characteristic distribution in household contacts
[LLM DRAFT] Generalized erythema and scaling affecting more than 90 percent of the body surface area
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with generalized erythema and scaling rather than tense subepidermal bullae.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by painful, dermatomal vesicular eruptions rather than widespread, tense pruritic blisters.
[LLM DRAFT] Features intense pruritus with burrows typically in web spaces, often affecting multiple household members, unlike autoimmune blistering.

[LLM DRAFT] Located typically over the medial malleolus with irregular borders and associated signs of venous hypertension, unlike neuropathic or pressure-related diabetic ulcers on plantar pressure points.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents as intensely pruritic, erythematous, and lichenified plaques rather than a localized, punched-out cutaneous breach on the foot.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales, commonly on extensor surfaces, rather than a full-thickness break in the skin of the foot.

[LLM DRAFT] Occurs after sun exposure without the direct trigger of a culprit medication, typically showing hard papules or plaques rather than a purely chemical phototoxic or photoallergic distribution.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with chronic, pruritic eczematous lesions in typical flexural folds rather than strictly sun-exposed areas.
[LLM DRAFT] Involves generalized erythema and scaling affecting over 90 percent of the body surface area, rather than being confined to sun-exposed regions.
[LLM DRAFT] Soft, mobile subcutaneous mass lacking a central punctum or expression of keratinaceous debris.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of classic thick silvery scales, well-demarcated plaques, and nail pitting or past history of plaque psoriasis before generalized erythroderma.
[LLM DRAFT] History of chronic pruritus, flexural lichenification, and IgE-mediated personal or family atopic diathesis preceding the generalized exfoliation.
[LLM DRAFT] Prominent facial edema, systemic involvement with fever, lymphadenopathy, atypical lymphocytosis, and internal organ dysfunction (e.g., hepatitis).
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with scattered, non-dermatomal mucocutaneous lesions lacking the characteristic grouped vesicles on an erythematous base seen in zoster.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by intense nocturnal pruritus and burrows in typical interdigital and flexor areas rather than painful dermatomal vesicles.
[LLM DRAFT] Firm, mobile dermal nodule often featuring a central punctum and foul-smelling keratinous discharge, unlike the softer, deeper consistency of a lipoma.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents as an acute sunburn-like reaction or photo-distributed erythema often linked to medication use, rather than chronic asymptomatic hyperpigmented macules.
[LLM DRAFT] Characterized by delayed, itchy polymorphic skin eruptions (papules, vesicles, or plaques) appearing hours to days after sun exposure, unlike the flat hyperpigmented patches of melasma.
[LLM DRAFT] Demonstrates fungal elements on KOH preparation or periodic acid-Schiff staining, whereas nail psoriasis is negative.
[LLM DRAFT] Accompanied by classic well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales on extensor surfaces and scalp.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of pitting, oil drop discoloration, and salmon patches without fungal elements on microscopy or culture.
[LLM DRAFT] Associated with classic plaque psoriasis skin lesions elsewhere on the body, aiding in the differentiation of nail involvement.
[LLM DRAFT] Associated with generalized pruritic eczematous skin lesions rather than isolated primary nail plate dystrophy.
[LLM DRAFT] Intense nocturnal pruritus with burrows, often in web spaces, whereas early yaws lesions are typically less itchy and manifest as papules or framboesial macules.
[LLM DRAFT] Presence of localized vesicular or exanthematous viral eruptions that typically resolve more rapidly than the persistent granulomatous lesions of early yaws.
[LLM DRAFT] Generalized erythema and scaling affecting over 90% of the body surface area, unlike the discrete, localized early cutaneous lesions characteristic of yaws.
[LLM DRAFT] Dermatomal distribution of painful vesicles clustered unilaterally rather than scattered or generalized lesions.
[LLM DRAFT] Lacks specific diagnostic features or viral identification to categorize it into a more defined viral exanthem or enanthem.
[LLM DRAFT] History of exposure in endemic regions with characteristic raspberry-like papillomatous lesions yielding positive darkfield microscopy or serology.
[LLM DRAFT] History of new medications or systemic photosensitizing agents preceding sun-exposed skin eruptions.
[LLM DRAFT] Pruritic eczematous lesions typically involving flexural creases rather than exclusively sun-exposed areas.
[LLM DRAFT] Pruritic erythematous patches typically affecting flexural creases rather than extensor surfaces.
[LLM DRAFT] Generalized erythema and scaling involving virtually the entire skin surface, often accompanied by systemic symptoms.
[LLM DRAFT] Presents with characteristic nail bed changes such as oil drops and pitting, which can mimic or accompany cutaneous psoriasis.
[LLM DRAFT] Pruritic eczematous patches often in flexural creases without burrows.
[LLM DRAFT] Generalized erythema and scaling covering most of the body surface area, seen in crusted scabies.
[LLM DRAFT] Tense subepidermal blisters typically occurring in elderly patients, distinct from mite burrows.
[LLM DRAFT] Located typically over pressure points and bony prominences rather than the gaiter area, often in the setting of peripheral neuropathy.
[LLM DRAFT] Melasma presents as acquired hyperpigmentation rather than complete depigmentation and typically affects sun-exposed areas of the face.
[LLM DRAFT] Psoriasis vulgaris features well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales, unlike the flat, depigmented macules of vitiligo.
[LLM DRAFT] Atopic dermatitis presents with pruritic, eczematous, erythematous lesions often with lichenification, rather than sharply marginated chalk-white macules.
